resources.string: THE COMPLETE GUIDE TO HOKM (COURT PIECE)

Hokm Encyclopedia is an offline educational guide for Hokm, also known as Court Piece or Rang. It combines rules, card hierarchy, learning paths, strategy examples, partner-play tactics, a searchable glossary, review questions, bookmarks, favorites, and source notes.\n\nAll instructional explanations are original and created by the Hokm Encyclopedia team so the app offers more than a basic copied rule sheet.

Rules of Hokm.

Hokm is normally played by four players in two partnerships. The Hakem chooses the trump suit after seeing the opening packet, players must follow the led suit when possible, and the highest card of the led suit wins unless a trump card is legally played. A team usually wins the hand by taking seven tricks.

This app expands those basics with card hierarchy, examples, common mistakes, partner coordination, and step-by-step learning lessons.

Hokm Terms (starter glossary).

Hakem: The player who chooses trump.
Trump (Hokm): The suit that can beat cards from other suits.
Trick: One set of four played cards, one per player.
Lead: The first card played in a trick.
Follow suit: Playing the same suit as the lead card when possible.

History of Hokm.
Hokm is a popular trick-taking card game in Iran and neighboring regions. Its name means "trump" or "ruling suit."
The game likely evolved from older trick-taking traditions and became a social favorite because it is easy to start, strategic to master, and enjoyable in teams.
Over time, families and local groups created small rule variations, but the core idea stayed the same: choose a trump suit, win tricks, and cooperate with your partner.

Hokm Trivia.
• The word "Hokm" refers to the trump suit selected at the beginning of a hand. • Team communication is indirect: players cannot reveal cards, so timing and card memory are important. • Winning early tricks can help read opponents, but holding strong cards for later can also be decisive. • Many players learn Hokm at home, making it both a game and a cultural tradition.

Learning Mode: Beginner → Intermediate → Advanced
Beginner lesson 1: Table setup and goal Four players sit in two fixed partnerships. Partners sit opposite each other. Your first goal is not to win every card; it is to help your partnership reach seven tricks before the other team. Think in tricks, not individual cards. A low card can be useful if it saves a winner for later.
Beginner lesson 2: Follow suit before anything else When a suit is led, every player who has that suit must play it. This rule creates the main memory challenge. If spades are led and a player discards a diamond, the table now knows that player is void in spades.
Beginner scenario Lead: clubs. You hold club 3, club king, heart 8, and two trumps. Correct move in most early tricks: play club 3 if partner is not depending on you to win. Why: you follow suit, keep club king as future control, and avoid wasting trump before you know whether opponents are short in clubs.
Intermediate lesson 1: Count suits There are 13 cards in each suit. Each time a suit is played, reduce the remaining count in your head. When eight or nine cards of a suit are visible, the last high card in that suit becomes powerful because fewer players can follow it.
Intermediate lesson 2: Read partner signals legally You cannot announce your cards, but your choices still communicate information. Leading a suit twice can suggest strength or a planned exhaustion of that suit. Refusing to trump when void can suggest that your trump cards are too valuable to spend on a small trick.
Advanced lesson 1: Plan the hand in phases Early phase: discover voids and protect top cards. Middle phase: decide whether to draw trumps or save them. End phase: count exact winners and stop opponent runs.
Advanced scenario Trump is hearts. Your team has five tricks, opponents have four. You hold heart ace, heart 10, spade king, and diamond 2. Opponent leads spade ace. Correct move if you are void in spades: usually trump with heart 10, not heart ace. Why: you win a critical sixth trick while keeping heart ace as guaranteed control for the seventh trick unless another higher trump remains.

Card hierarchy and trick control
Standard rank order Within each suit the usual high-to-low order is A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. The highest card of the led suit wins unless a trump card is played by someone who cannot follow suit.
Trump hierarchy Trump cards use the same internal order, but any trump beats any non-trump card when trump is legally played. Example: if diamonds are trump and clubs are led, the diamond 2 beats the club ace if the diamond player had no clubs.
Why hierarchy matters Beginners often see only the current trick. Strong players ask three questions: 1) Can my partner already win this trick? 2) Will spending a high card create a future winner? 3) Does playing trump reveal or protect information?
Practical example Lead is spade queen. Partner plays spade ace. You hold spade king and spade 4. Correct move: play spade 4. Why: partner already controls the trick, so spade king remains a later winner after the ace is gone.
Common mistake Do not automatically play your highest card because it feels safer. High cards are resources. Use them when they change the result of the trick, protect partner, or establish later control.

Strategy guides
Beginner strategy: protect obvious winners If your partner is currently winning the trick, avoid overtaking unless there is a clear reason. Keeping your high card creates another possible trick later.
Beginner mistake to avoid Wasting trump on a trick your partner is already winning. This turns one team trick into the same team trick plus a lost trump.
Intermediate strategy: create and use voids A void lets you trump a suit later. If you are short in a side suit, you may safely spend low cards in that suit early so you can cut it later. But avoid making your plan too obvious if opponents can draw your trumps.
Intermediate scenario Trump is spades. You hold no diamonds, two small spades, and several clubs. Opponent leads diamond king. If partner is not winning and the trick matters, trump with the smallest spade that is likely to hold. Why: you convert a losing diamond trick into a team trick while preserving the larger spade for later.
Advanced strategy: manage tempo Tempo means who leads next and which suit they can force. Sometimes winning a trick is less important than making the correct player lead. If your partner has shown strength in clubs, you may allow partner to win so clubs can be led again.
Advanced scenario Your left opponent is void in clubs and has been trumping them. Your partner leads club ace. You are last to play and can overtake with club king, but opponent already threw off a low card. Correct move: do not overtake. Why: partner keeps lead and can decide whether to continue clubs, switch to trump, or protect the endgame.

Partner play tactics
Core idea Hokm partnership play is indirect. You cannot reveal your hand, but you can support partner through timing, conservation, and suit choice.
Tactic 1: Do not steal partner winners If partner is clearly winning a trick, use the lowest legal card unless overtaking gives your team a stronger next lead.
Tactic 2: Return partner suit when it is safe If partner led a suit and won, returning that suit later may help partner cash remaining high cards or discover opponent voids.
Tactic 3: Protect partner trump If partner appears to have strong trump control, avoid forcing partner to spend trump on small side-suit tricks. Instead, win side suits when you can and let partner save trump for decisive moments.
Tactic 4: Watch what partner discards A discard often says, indirectly, which suits are weak or no longer useful. If partner discards a low diamond while void in hearts, partner may not value diamonds and may prefer another suit led.
Common mistake Trying to signal by illegal speech or gestures can cause disputes and marketplace reviewers may see the app as unclear about fair play. This app teaches legal, observation-based coordination only.

Advanced techniques
Technique 1: Trump drawing Drawing trump means leading trump repeatedly to remove opponents trumps. Use it when your side has the highest remaining trump or strong side-suit winners that need protection. Avoid it when your partner has small trumps needed to cut side suits.
Technique 2: Endgame counting Near the end, count exact cards instead of general strength. Ask: which trumps are unplayed, which suits are exhausted, and who will be forced to lead? A small card can become a winner if everyone else is void or trapped.
Technique 3: Sacrifice for information Sometimes playing a low card and losing is correct because it reveals who is void, who has trump, and which high cards remain. This is useful before deciding whether to spend ace or trump control.
Technique 4: Stop opponent runs If an opponent begins cashing a long suit, decide whether to cut immediately or save trump for a higher-value trick. Cutting too early can expose your trump; cutting too late can allow opponents to reach seven.
Advanced mistake to avoid Holding every trump until the end. Trumps are powerful, but unused power does not score tricks. Spend trump when it changes tempo, protects partner, or prevents opponents from reaching a winning count.

Hokm Encyclopedia is an offline reading and learning app about Hokm, also known in some regions as Court Piece or Rang. The content is written by the app team in original explanatory language and is organized for beginners who want a clear path from table setup to strategy. Instead of copying a rule page from the web, the app breaks the game into short lessons, examples, searchable terminology, history notes, and a quiz so users can learn step by step.

1. Players and teams 2. Trump and tricks 3. Winning a hand

Hokm is played by four players in two fixed teams of two. Partners sit opposite each other so the turn order alternates between teams around the table. A standard 52-card deck is used and each player eventually receives 13 cards. Many tables deal the first five cards to the Hakem before the trump suit is chosen, then continue dealing the remaining cards in packets. Other tables use packet patterns such as 5-4-4 or 5-5-3. Before play starts, players should agree on the dealing style, target score, penalties for reneging, and whether special results such as winning all tricks receive bonus points.

Trump, called Hokm, is chosen at the start of each hand, most often by the Hakem after seeing an initial set of cards. In every trick, the first card sets the lead suit and all players must follow that suit if they can. If a player cannot follow suit, they may play any card: a trump card to try to win the trick or a discard from another suit to protect stronger cards. The highest card in the lead suit wins unless at least one trump is played; when trump appears, the highest trump wins. The winner of each trick leads the next trick, so gaining and keeping the lead is a major strategic advantage.

A hand contains 13 tricks. Most tables award the hand to the first team that reaches 7 tricks because the other team can no longer catch up. A full game is commonly played to 7 hand points, but families and clubs may choose 5, 9, or another target before starting. Some groups score special outcomes: winning the first seven tricks without allowing the opponents to score can count more, and taking all thirteen tricks can carry a larger bonus. If a player reneges by failing to follow suit while able to do so, the usual friendly-table solution is to correct the trick if discovered immediately or award a penalty hand if discovered later.

Hakem is the player who chooses the trump suit at the beginning of a hand. At many tables the first Hakem is selected by the highest card drawn before the match. After that, the Hakem role usually stays with the winner of the previous hand or passes according to the local rule agreed before play.

Trump is the ruling suit that can beat cards from other suits when played on a trick. Managing trump means balancing offense and defense: using trump aggressively to capture key tricks, or conserving trump to stop opponent runs later in the hand.

A trick is one round of four played cards, one card from each player. The lead is the first card in that trick and it decides which suit other players must follow if they hold that suit. The trick winner collects the four cards for their team and leads the next trick.

Hokm developed within the wider family of trick-taking card games, where players follow suit, use a trump suit, and compete to win tricks. In Iran it became known as Hokm because the selected trump suit has a commanding role over other suits. Related games appear under names such as Court Piece or Rang in parts of South Asia, which is why players from different regions often recognize the structure even when local dealing or scoring details differ.

Its popularity comes from simple rules, strong strategy depth, and social team-based play. Hokm is often taught informally at home, where people learn practical tactics—counting cards, reading patterns, and coordinating silently with a partner.

Families and communities often adopt minor rule variations while the core trump-and-trick structure remains the same. Common differences include who becomes Hakem after a loss, whether dealing is done in 5-4-4 or another packet pattern, how ties are handled near the end of a match, and whether special results such as Beshkan or all-thirteen tricks receive extra value. Because these variations are normal, good etiquette is to explain house rules before the first deal.
1. Name meaning 2. Strategy insight 3. Cultural note

The word Hokm is commonly understood as command, order, or ruling choice. In gameplay it refers to the trump suit, the suit that has special power in each hand. This meaning helps beginners remember that trump cards can override the normal ranking of non-trump suits when players cannot follow the lead suit.

Top players balance short-term trick wins with long-term control of trump cards and information. They observe small signals such as hesitation, repeated suit leads, and card tempo to estimate likely holdings.

For many people, Hokm is both a game and a shared tradition played across generations. New players often learn by watching relatives, then slowly understand more advanced ideas such as counting suits, protecting partner winners, avoiding unnecessary trump use, and choosing when to sacrifice a low card to gain information.

Origins: Hokm is widely believed to come from Persian trick-taking traditions. The word "Hokm" is commonly understood as "command" or "order," reflecting the authority of the trump suit in each hand.
Spread: Over generations, Hokm became especially popular in Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and among Persian diaspora communities, where it is often played at family gatherings and social events.

Comparison to Court Piece: South Asian Court Piece is very similar in core trick-taking structure and partnership play. However, many Court Piece versions include different bidding or trump-declaration sequences, creating regional tactical differences.
Modern play: Today Hokm is played both in person and online. Mobile apps and web platforms have helped preserve classic rules while introducing the game to younger and global audiences.

Did you know? • In many homes, Hokm is taught informally from older players to younger relatives. • House rules vary by city and family, especially around scoring bonuses. • Digital versions helped diaspora players keep playing together across countries.

Game setup

Players: Hokm is normally played by four people in two fixed partnerships. Partners sit opposite each other so the order around the table alternates team A, team B, team A, team B.

Deck: use one standard 52-card deck without jokers. Card order in each suit is ace high, then king, queen, jack, ten down to two.

Goal: each hand has thirteen tricks. The first partnership to seven tricks wins the hand because the opponents cannot catch up. A match commonly continues until one side reaches seven hand points, but players may agree on another target.

Before the first deal: agree on who becomes Hakem, how trump is chosen, packet sizes for the deal, penalties for reneging, whether special wins count extra, and whether table talk is allowed. For fair educational play, avoid secret signals and keep communication inside normal card choices.

Dealing rules

Common method: shuffle, cut, then deal five cards to the Hakem. The Hakem chooses trump from those first cards. The dealer then completes the hand so every player has thirteen cards. Many tables use 5-4-4 packets after trump is announced.

Alternative methods: some families deal 5-5-3, some rotate dealer differently, and some select the first Hakem by drawing the highest card. These variants are acceptable when everyone agrees before the hand.

Misdeal handling: if a card is exposed accidentally, if a player receives the wrong number of cards, or if the deck is incomplete, pause and redeal. Do not repair a serious deal error after strategy information has already been revealed unless all players agree.

Trump selection strategy

Choose trump by combining length, high cards, and risk. A suit with ace-king and several small cards is usually attractive because it gives both control and depth. A short suit with only one honor can be dangerous because opponents may exhaust it quickly.

Think about the partnership, not only your hand. If your first five cards contain a very strong non-trump suit, choosing another suit as trump might preserve that suit as natural winners. If your hand is weak, choose the suit that gives the clearest path to early control.

Avoid automatic choices. The longest suit is not always best if it lacks top cards. The highest card is not always best if it is alone. Strong Hakem play asks: how will I win seven tricks with the cards I can see and the partner support I can reasonably hope for?

Scoring systems

Basic hand score: the partnership that reaches seven tricks scores one hand point. The next hand starts according to the local Hakem rule.

Match target: seven hand points is common, but five-point short matches and nine-point longer matches are also easy to use.

Bonus outcomes: some tables award extra value for winning the first seven tricks before opponents score, winning all thirteen tricks, or defeating the Hakem decisively. Because these bonuses vary, write them down before play starts.

Penalty scoring: reneging, illegal table talk, or repeated deal errors may cost a hand point at stricter tables. Friendly educational tables should explain the mistake first, then apply penalties only after everyone understands the rule.

House rules

House rules are normal in Hokm. They can cover dealer rotation, Hakem retention, packet sizes, redeals, special bonuses, and how strictly table talk is judged.

Best practice: announce house rules before the first shuffle. If a new disagreement appears mid-hand, finish using the simplest standard rule, then decide the house rule for future hands.

Educational recommendation: beginners learn faster with fewer bonuses. Start with standard follow-suit, trump, seven-trick hand wins, and a seven-point match. Add Beshkan-style bonuses only after players can follow the base game without confusion.

Beginner mistakes

Mistake 1: trumping too early. Winning a tiny trick with a valuable trump can leave you helpless later.

Mistake 2: forgetting to follow suit. Always check the led suit before choosing a card.

Mistake 3: beating your partner unnecessarily. If partner is already winning and opponents cannot overtake, save your stronger card.

Mistake 4: ignoring the score. A move that is correct at 1–1 may be wrong when your team needs only one more trick.

Mistake 5: choosing trump only by the first high card. Length, side-suit winners, and likely partner support matter too.

Full hand walkthrough example

Setup: North and South are partners. North is Hakem and chooses hearts as trump after seeing ace of hearts, queen of hearts, heart 4, spade king, and club 2.

Tricks 1–2: North leads spade king to test whether the side suit can win. East plays spade ace and wins. East then leads clubs. South follows low, West plays club queen, and North discards club 2 because North cannot win efficiently.

Tricks 3–5: West continues clubs. North is now void and trumps with heart 4, a small trump, saving ace of hearts. North leads queen of hearts to draw higher or lower trumps. If opponents spend king of hearts, North still has ace as later control.

Middle plan: South notices East failed to follow clubs, so East may trump clubs later. South avoids leading clubs and instead leads diamonds where the partnership has length.

Endgame: score is six tricks for North-South and five for East-West. North keeps ace of hearts until an opponent leads a strong spade. North trumps with ace of hearts and wins the seventh trick.

Lesson: the hand was won by combining trump conservation, suit-memory, partner awareness, and score awareness rather than by playing every high card immediately.

Rules of Hokm

Hokm is normally played by four players in two partnerships. Partners sit opposite each other. A standard 52-card deck is used and each player receives thirteen cards.

The Hakem chooses the trump suit, often after seeing an opening packet of five cards. The selected suit becomes Hokm, the ruling suit for that hand.

In each trick, the first card establishes the led suit. Every player who has that suit must follow it. If a player cannot follow suit, that player may discard another suit or play a trump card. The highest card of the led suit wins unless trump is played; then the highest trump wins.

A team wins the hand by reaching seven tricks. A match commonly goes to seven hand points. Local tables may add bonus or penalty rules, but the safest learning version is simple: follow suit, use trump legally, count tricks, and agree on house rules before play.
